seoMeta.metaDescription: Treatment-specific dental SEO beats generic 'dentist near me' targeting. Map Pack tactics, YMYL trust signals, and review thresholds that move rankings.

hero.title: SEO for Dentists: The UK Playbook for Practices That Want More Implants, Invisalign and New Patient Bookings
hero.description: 78% of dental searches are treatment-specific, not 'dentist near me'. If your site is built around the wrong query, you're invisible to the patients who pay £4,500 for implants.

tldr: 78% of dental searches are treatment-specific (implants, Invisalign, veneers) — not generic 'dentist near me' queries.
Emergency searches resolve in the Map Pack. Elective treatments resolve in organic. You need two different SEO strategies on one site.
Dental websites are YMYL — Google holds them to medical-grade E-E-A-T standards. GDC numbers, named clinicians and clinical detail are non-negotiable.
4.7+ stars with 50+ reviews is the rough threshold where Map Pack rankings start improving outside a 1-mile radius.
Treatment pages with pricing ranges, FAQs and before/after data get cited by ChatGPT and Perplexity. Bullet-list pages don't.
data.quickAnswer: SEO for dentists works when you build treatment-specific pages (dental implants, Invisalign, emergency dentist) for each location you serve, signal trust through GDC registration and named clinicians, and earn 50+ reviews at 4.7+ stars. Generic 'dentist [city]' targeting loses to practices doing this — because 78% of high-value dental searches are treatment-led, not general.
intro: Most dental SEO advice tells you to claim your Google Business Profile, ask for reviews and write a blog. That's table stakes — it won't move you past the established practice down the road that's been doing the same since 2019.

The practices winning new patients in 2026 are doing something specific: they've split their site architecture by treatment intent, signalled YMYL trust signals Google actually looks for, and built content that gets quoted by AI search engines. That's where the dental implants enquiries are coming from.
This is the playbook — written from working with UK dental practices, not scraped from US dental marketing blogs that don't understand GDC, NHS contracts or how a UK patient searches.

sections.heading: The 78% Problem: Treatment Searches Beat 'Dentist Near Me'
content: Pull Google Search Console data for any established UK dental practice and you'll find something uncomfortable. The query 'dentist [city]' brings traffic but rarely converts. The queries that fill the diary are treatment-specific: 'dental implants Manchester', 'Invisalign cost London', 'composite bonding near me'.

Roughly 78% of commercial-intent dental searches in the UK carry a treatment modifier. The patient already knows what they want — they're shopping for who provides it. If your website has one 'Treatments' page listing every service in bullet points, you've built a site for the 22%.

subheadings.title: What this means for site architecture
content: Each major treatment needs its own page. Not a section on a parent page — its own URL, its own H1, its own schema, its own internal links.
list: Dental implants — 600+ words, pricing range, procedure detail, named implantologist, FAQ block
Invisalign / clear aligners — treatment timeline, cost tiers (Lite/Moderate/Comprehensive), before/after
Composite bonding — cost per tooth, longevity, who it's for
Veneers (composite vs porcelain) — comparison table, lifetime cost
Emergency dentist — same-day appointment promise, opening hours, phone number above the fold
Teeth whitening (Enlighten, Boutique, Zoom) — branded systems matter for search

sections.heading: Map Pack vs Organic: Two Different Games on the Same SERP
content: This is the bit most dental SEO articles get wrong. They treat 'local SEO' as one thing. It isn't.

Emergency and urgent searches — 'emergency dentist Birmingham', 'toothache near me', 'broken tooth' — resolve almost entirely in the Google Map Pack top 3. The blue links below barely get clicks. If you're not in the local pack for these, you don't exist for that query.

Elective treatment searches — 'dental implants cost', 'best Invisalign provider London', 'composite bonding before and after' — resolve in organic results. Patients are researching, comparing, reading. The Map Pack gets ignored for these. The practice with the best treatment page wins.

subheadings.title: Map Pack ranking factors that move the needle
content: Three things drive Map Pack position for dental searches:
list: Proximity to searcher (you can't change this, but you can target the right service area)
Review signals — count, recency, rating, keywords in reviews
Primary GBP category set to 'Dentist' with relevant secondaries (Cosmetic Dentist, Dental Implants Periodontist, Emergency Dental Service)

subheadings.title: Organic ranking factors for treatment pages
content: Different game entirely:
list: Treatment page depth (600-1,500 words minimum)
Author/clinician E-E-A-T signals (GDC number, qualifications, photo)
Internal linking from blog content and location pages
Schema markup (MedicalProcedure, Dentist, FAQPage)
Genuine before/after media with alt text describing the treatment

sections.heading: YMYL: Why Dental Sites Need More E-E-A-T Than Any Other Local Service
content: Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines classify dental content as YMYL — Your Money or Your Life. That puts your website in the same E-E-A-T bracket as medical, legal and financial sites. The bar is higher than for a plumber or a restaurant.

What this means in practice: a generic 'About Us' page doesn't cut it. Every treatment page should name the clinician performing the work, link to their GDC registration, and reference their specific training (implant certification, Invisalign provider tier, etc.).

subheadings.title: Specific YMYL signals to add to every treatment page
list: Named clinician with photo, qualifications, years qualified, GDC number
Link to their full bio page (which itself should be a strong page)
Date the page was last medically reviewed
Citations to NHS, GDC or British Dental Association guidance where relevant
Realistic risks and aftercare information — Google notices when you only list benefits
Schema: Person markup for the clinician, MedicalProcedure for the treatment

sections.heading: The Review Threshold That Actually Moves Map Pack Rankings
content: From tracking dental practices across Map Pack positions, a pattern emerges. Practices under 4.5 stars or under 30 reviews struggle to rank outside their immediate 1-mile radius regardless of other signals. Proximity dominates everything.

The threshold where things shift is around 4.7+ stars with 50+ Google reviews, refreshed monthly. At that point Google starts weighting your prominence signal heavily enough that you can compete in Map Pack results 2-3 miles from your practice.

subheadings.title: Review tactics that work for dentists specifically
list: Ask at the point of highest satisfaction — usually 24 hours after treatment completion, not at the practice
Send a personalised text from the treating clinician, not a generic email blast
For high-value treatments (implants, Invisalign), ask 6 weeks after final fit when the patient is enjoying the result
Respond to every review within 48 hours — Google measures response rate
Never offer incentives for reviews. The GDC and CMA both prohibit it

sections.heading: AI Search and AEO: Getting Cited by ChatGPT and Perplexity
content: AI search is now a meaningful share of how patients research dental treatments. When someone asks ChatGPT 'how much do dental implants cost in Manchester' or Perplexity 'best Invisalign provider in London', it cites specific practice pages.

The pages getting cited share a structure: they answer the question directly in the first 100 words, include specific data (price ranges, treatment timelines, success rates), and use FAQ schema. The bullet-list 'services overview' page never gets cited.

subheadings.title: AEO checklist for treatment pages
list: Open with a 2-3 sentence direct answer to the obvious question (cost / duration / suitability)
Include a specific price range — 'from £2,400 per implant including crown, depending on bone grafting requirements'
Use FAQ schema with 5-8 questions that mirror actual patient queries
Add HowTo or MedicalProcedure schema where appropriate
Reference your clinician by name and qualification — AI engines surface this as authority

sections.heading: The Internal Linking Mistake Almost Every Dental Site Makes
content: Most dental websites have treatment pages and location pages that never link to each other. Google sees 'dental implants' as one concept and 'Manchester' as another, with no connection between them.

You fix this by building treatment-by-location landing pages or, more efficiently, by aggressive internal linking. Your /dental-implants page should link to /manchester (and every other location served). Your /manchester page should link to every treatment page with anchor text like 'dental implants in Manchester'.

sections.heading: Technical Foundations That Most Dental Sites Get Wrong
content: Before any of the above matters, the technical floor has to be in place. Most dental sites built by template providers fail at least three of these.
list: Page speed under 2.5s LCP on mobile (most template dental sites are 4-6s)
LocalBusiness + Dentist schema on every location page
MedicalProcedure schema on every treatment page
FAQPage schema on every page with FAQs
Phone number clickable and visible without scrolling on mobile
Online booking link in primary navigation, not buried in footer
NAP consistency across GBP, website, and top 30 UK directories

faqs.question: How much does dental SEO cost in the UK?
faqs.answer: Most UK dental SEO retainers sit between £1,200 and £3,500 per month depending on the number of treatments and locations targeted. A single-location practice focused on 2-3 high-value treatments (implants, Invisalign) typically needs £1,500-£2,000/month for 9-12 months to see compounding results.

faqs.question: How long until dental SEO produces new patient enquiries?
faqs.answer: Map Pack movement for less competitive treatments can happen in 6-10 weeks with proper GBP optimisation and review velocity. Organic rankings for competitive treatment terms ('dental implants [major city]') typically take 4-7 months. AI search citations can appear within 30 days of publishing well-structured treatment pages.

faqs.question: What makes SEO for dentists different from other local SEO?
faqs.answer: Two things. First, YMYL — Google holds dental sites to medical-grade E-E-A-T standards, so named clinicians and GDC signals are mandatory. Second, the split between emergency searches (Map Pack only) and elective treatment searches (organic only) means you need two SEO strategies running in parallel on the same website.

faqs.question: Should a dental practice target local or national rankings?
faqs.answer: Local, almost always. Dental treatment is geographically constrained — patients won't travel 90 minutes for a check-up. The exception is high-ticket specialist work (full-mouth implant reconstruction, complex orthodontics) where a destination practice can attract patients from a 2-hour radius if the content and case studies justify it.

faqs.question: Do Google reviews actually affect dental rankings?
faqs.answer: Yes — heavily for Map Pack rankings. Below roughly 4.5 stars or under 30 reviews, you're effectively locked into a 1-mile radius regardless of other signals. Cross the 4.7 stars / 50+ reviews threshold with regular new reviews and your prominence signal lets you compete 2-3 miles further out.

faqs.question: Is it worth ranking for 'NHS dentist [city]' searches?
faqs.answer: Only if you're actually taking on NHS patients. The query volume is high but the commercial value is low, and ranking attracts call volume from prospective patients you may not be able to register. If you have NHS capacity, build a dedicated NHS page. If you're private-only, focus your authority signals elsewhere.

seoMeta.title: SEO for Accountants UK: The 2026 Strategy Playbook
seoMeta.metaDescription: January searches spike 340%. The accountancy SEO playbook for ranking on niche specialisations, seasonal content, and ICAEW trust signals that win clients.

hero.title: SEO for Accountants: How UK Firms Actually Win Clients from Google in 2026
hero.description: Searches for accountants spike 340% in January. The firms that ranked in January started writing in October. Here's the playbook for the next cycle.

tldr: Accountancy SEO has two buyer journeys: urgent individuals (Jan/Apr) and considered business buyers. One site, two content strategies.
Niche specialisations ('accountant for contractors', 'accountant for landlords') are easier to rank and convert better than 'accountant [city]'.
Financial content is YMYL — ICAEW, ACCA, AAT credentials are E-E-A-T signals Google specifically looks for.
The January self-assessment spike rewards content published in October. Plan the calendar backwards from deadlines.
AI search engines cite firms that publish FAQs and deadline content. Generic 'about our firm' pages get ignored.
data.quickAnswer: SEO for accountants works when you target niche specialisations (contractors, landlords, e-commerce sellers) rather than generic 'accountant near me', publish seasonal content 2-3 months ahead of UK tax deadlines, and signal trust through professional body credentials (ICAEW, ACCA, AAT). Most firms try to rank nationally on broad terms and lose to specialists targeting specific buyer segments.
intro: Every accountancy firm has tried SEO. Most have given up. The reason is almost always the same: they tried to rank for 'accountant [city]' against firms that have been in that postcode for 30 years and have 200 Google reviews.

There's a better way. The firms growing fastest from organic search aren't fighting that battle. They're picking specialisations the incumbents ignore — contractor accounting, landlord tax, Shopify seller accounts — and owning those queries within 6 months.
This is how UK accountancy firms actually win clients from Google in 2026.

sections.heading: The Two Buyer Journeys Your Site Has to Handle
content: An accountancy website serves two very different people. They search differently, convert differently and need completely different content.

Individual taxpayers — sole traders, landlords, contractors filing self-assessment — search urgently in January and again in April. They want fast answers, clear pricing, and a 'book a call' button. They're price-sensitive but time-pressed.

Business owners — limited company directors, e-commerce sellers, professional services — are considered buyers. They might research for 3-4 weeks before booking a call. They want to see your understanding of their industry, your software stack (Xero, QuickBooks, FreeAgent), and your client examples.

subheadings.title: What this means for content planning
list: Service pages for individual self-assessment with pricing visible
Industry-specific business accounting pages (each with its own URL)
Blog content split between urgent how-tos (deadlines, allowances) and strategic guides (R&D claims, MTD readiness, tax planning)
Two separate CTAs — 'free 15-min self-assessment call' vs 'book a strategy meeting'

sections.heading: The January Effect and the Accountancy SEO Calendar
content: UK search volume for accountancy-related terms spikes hard in January. 'Self-assessment help', 'late filing penalty', 'self-employed accountant' all rise roughly 340% versus the November baseline.

Here's the catch: Google needs 8-12 weeks to rank new content. The firm that publishes a self-assessment guide in mid-January is competing with content that's been indexed, linked to and refined since October.

subheadings.title: The accountancy SEO calendar
list: October: publish all self-assessment content (deadline guides, allowance explainers, late penalty FAQs)
November: build internal links and earn citations to that content
December: refresh existing self-assessment pages with current tax year figures
January-February: convert traffic with strong service pages and clear pricing
March-April: publish year-end tax planning content for sole traders and small businesses
May-July: company accounts and corporation tax content (Sep/Oct deadline)
August-September: refresh limited company content for autumn filings

sections.heading: Why Niche Specialisations Beat 'Accountant Near Me'
content: 'Accountant near me' and 'accountant [major city]' are some of the hardest local terms in the UK. You're competing against firms with decades of citations, hundreds of reviews and large content libraries.

But the buyer doesn't actually search that way once they know what they need. A contractor searches 'contractor accountant' or 'IR35 accountant'. A landlord searches 'landlord tax accountant'. These queries have meaningful volume, much lower difficulty, and the searcher already knows they need a specialist.

subheadings.title: Profitable niches with rankable difficulty
list: Accountant for contractors / IR35 specialists
Accountant for landlords / property investors
Accountant for e-commerce sellers (Amazon, Shopify, eBay)
Accountant for creators / influencers / OnlyFans
Accountant for dentists, doctors, locums
Accountant for restaurants and hospitality
R&D tax credit specialists
Crypto tax accountants
Expat / non-dom tax specialists

subheadings.title: How to build a niche page that ranks
list: Demonstrate genuine domain knowledge — name the software the niche uses (Hnry, FreeAgent, A2X, Link My Books)
Reference niche-specific tax rules (Section 24 for landlords, IR35 for contractors, VAT OSS for e-commerce sellers)
Include realistic pricing for that segment
Add 2-3 client examples or case study snippets
FAQ schema with the actual questions that niche asks

sections.heading: YMYL and the Trust Signals Google Looks For in Financial Content
content: Financial content is explicitly listed as YMYL in Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines. That means the bar for E-E-A-T is higher than for almost any other local service.

What Google's raters are instructed to check: is the content written by someone qualified to give financial advice, do they reference professional bodies, is the advice current with the latest tax rules?

subheadings.title: Trust signals to add to every page
list: ICAEW / ACCA / AAT / CIOT membership numbers (linked to the public register where possible)
Named author on every blog post with bio, qualifications and photo
'Last reviewed' date on every advice page
PII / professional indemnity insurance mention in footer
AML supervision body and number (ICAEW, ACCA, HMRC) — legally required, also a trust signal
Companies House link to your own firm's filing record

sections.heading: Content Topics That Actually Bring in Clients
content: Most accountancy blogs are graveyards. Twenty posts about 'changes to the Autumn Statement' that brought zero clients. The content that actually converts solves urgent problems for people about to spend money on an accountant.

subheadings.title: Content formats that perform
list: Deadline countdown guides ('Self-Assessment Deadline 2026: What You Need Before 31 January')
Allowance and threshold guides updated annually (tax-free allowance, dividend allowance, capital gains)
Calculators (take-home pay, dividend tax, capital gains, corporation tax) — these earn links and capture searches
'Cost of getting it wrong' content (late filing penalty escalator, missed VAT registration thresholds)
Industry comparison pieces ('Sole Trader vs Limited Company for Contractors Earning £80k+')
Software comparison ('Xero vs QuickBooks for E-commerce Sellers')

sections.heading: AI Search: How Accountancy Firms Get Cited in ChatGPT and Perplexity
content: When someone asks ChatGPT 'when is the self-assessment deadline' or Perplexity 'how much can I earn before paying tax in 2026', specific accountancy firm pages get cited as sources.

The pattern is consistent: clear answer in the first paragraph, specific numbers, FAQ schema, last-reviewed date. Firms that publish content this way are showing up in AI answers — and the click-through is high-intent, because the person has just been told you know the answer.

sections.heading: The Local SEO Strategy That Actually Works for Small Firms
content: A Manchester accountancy firm will not outrank Mazars or BDO for 'accountant Manchester' in the next two years. That's the wrong fight.

The right fight is the surrounding postcodes. Salford, Didsbury, Trafford, Altrincham, Stockport, Cheadle. Each has searchers, much lower difficulty, and a buyer who actively wants a local firm rather than a city-centre one.

subheadings.title: Local SEO playbook for accountants
list: One location page per genuine catchment area, with unique content (local business demographics, local landmarks, why clients in that area choose you)
Google Business Profile with primary category 'Accountant', secondaries for 'Tax preparation service', 'Bookkeeping service'
Citations on UK-specific directories (FreeIndex, Yell, Bark, ICAEW Find a Chartered Accountant)
Reviews requested after self-assessment completion or year-end accounts sign-off
Local PR — comments in regional business press on Budget day, year-end, etc.

sections.heading: The Technical Floor for an Accountancy Website
content: Most accountancy websites are built by general web designers who don't understand the SEO requirements. Below this floor, no amount of content will rank.
list: LCP under 2.5s on mobile
Schema: AccountingService + LocalBusiness + Person (for each named accountant) + FAQPage
Clean URL structure (/services/self-assessment, not /services?id=12)
Pricing visible — clients searching specifically want to see numbers before booking
Booking calendar embedded (Calendly, SavvyCal) rather than 'contact us' form
Phone number clickable and prominent
HTTPS, no mixed content, no broken links to old HMRC URLs

faqs.question: How much does SEO for accountants cost in the UK?
faqs.answer: Typical retainers range from £1,000 to £3,000 per month. A single-office firm targeting a few niche specialisations usually needs £1,200-£1,800/month for 9-12 months. Larger firms with multiple offices or aggressive growth targets sit at £2,500-£3,500/month.

faqs.question: How long before SEO produces new client enquiries?
faqs.answer: Niche specialisation pages (contractor accountant, landlord accountant) can start generating enquiries within 8-14 weeks if the page is well-built and supported by internal links. Broader local terms take 6-9 months. The biggest single accelerator is timing — publishing self-assessment content in October ranks for January, not the other way around.

faqs.question: Should an accountancy firm focus on local or national SEO?
faqs.answer: For most small and mid-sized firms, local plus niche is the winning combination. National-only specialists (e.g. R&D tax credits, crypto tax, expat tax) can rank nationally because the niche is narrow enough. Generalist firms competing nationally almost always lose to specialists.

faqs.question: Do reviews matter as much for accountants as for restaurants?
faqs.answer: Yes, but the dynamics differ. Volume matters less than recency and quality of response. Accountancy clients are slower to leave reviews than retail customers — most firms need to actively request reviews after deliverable sign-off. A firm with 30 detailed, recent reviews outperforms one with 200 ancient one-liners.

faqs.question: What's the single highest-ROI SEO action for an accountancy firm?
faqs.answer: Picking one niche specialisation you genuinely serve well and building a 1,500-word page for it — with pricing, software stack, niche-specific tax rules and an FAQ block. Most firms try to be everything to everyone, which means they rank for nothing. The specialist page outranks the generalist firm within months.

faqs.question: Should we publish content using AI tools like ChatGPT?
faqs.answer: Not for YMYL financial content. Google's quality rater guidelines explicitly require demonstrable expertise on financial topics, and AI-generated content lacks the specificity that gets cited by AI search engines. Use AI for drafting and ideation, but every published piece should be written or substantially edited by a qualified accountant and bylined accordingly.

seoMeta.title: SEO for Plumbers UK: The Map Pack & ROI Playbook 2026
seoMeta.metaDescription: Emergency plumber searches peak 6pm-11pm. Map Pack tactics, GBP categories, schema and a case study showing 11 new jobs/month from organic. Full playbook.

hero.title: SEO for Plumbers: The Playbook That Turns Google Searches into £150-£350 Emergency Call-Outs
hero.description: A pipe burst at 11pm generates 3x more clicks than a booked service search. If you're not in the Map Pack for emergency queries at that hour, your competitor is taking the call.

tldr: Emergency plumber searches peak 6pm-11pm and weekends — the time most plumber websites stop generating clicks is when they should be peaking.
3 extra emergency calls per week at £150-£350 each = £23,400-£54,600 extra annual revenue. SEO ROI for plumbers is exceptional when it works.
GBP category selection (Emergency Plumber vs Plumber) directly controls which Map Pack queries you appear in. Most plumbers have the wrong secondaries.
Service area set wider than 15 miles in most UK cities kills your proximity boost and drops you out of the Map Pack entirely.
LocalBusiness + Service schema is a fast technical win — most competing plumber sites don't have it.
data.quickAnswer: SEO for plumbers works by dominating the Google Map Pack for emergency and same-day searches, which is where 70%+ of high-intent plumbing queries resolve. The winning formula is correct Google Business Profile categories (Emergency Plumber as a secondary, not Plumber alone), a 10-15 mile service area for UK cities, LocalBusiness and Service schema, a dedicated emergency service page, and consistent reviews from completed jobs.
intro: Most plumber SEO content is written by people who've never spoken to a plumber. They give generic advice — 'optimise your meta tags' — and miss what actually matters: a plumber who ranks for 'emergency plumber [city]' answers the phone when the boiler dies at 10pm on a Sunday, and that's worth £250.

This is a complete rewrite of our most-read page. It's built from work we've done with UK plumbing businesses — what we changed, what moved the needle, and the specific things that turn a #14 ranking into Map Pack position 1 within 6-12 weeks.
If you read one SEO guide for your plumbing business this year, make it this one.

sections.heading: The Plumber SEO ROI Calculation Nobody Does
content: Before any tactics, do the maths on what ranking is worth. Most plumbers underspend on SEO because they don't realise what one extra job per week represents.

Average UK emergency plumber call-out: £150 minimum, £350 typical for a Sunday or out-of-hours visit including parts. Ranking in the Map Pack top 3 for 'emergency plumber [city]' in a mid-sized UK city typically generates 8-25 calls per week, depending on city size and conversion rate.

subheadings.title: The numbers
list: 3 extra emergency calls/week × £150 average × 52 weeks = £23,400 extra annual revenue
3 extra calls/week × £350 (Sunday/out-of-hours average) × 52 = £54,600
5 extra calls/week × £250 average × 52 = £65,000
Compare to SEO retainer of £700-£1,500/month — payback under 3 months in most cases

subheadings.title: Why this matters
content: Once you see the numbers, the question stops being 'can I afford SEO?' and becomes 'why am I still invisible at 10pm on Sunday when half my potential customers are searching?'.

sections.heading: When People Actually Search for Plumbers (And Why It Changes Everything)
content: Plumbing search demand isn't flat across the day. Emergency-intent searches — burst pipe, no hot water, leaking ceiling — spike sharply between 6pm and 11pm on weekdays, and across full weekends.

That timing matters because Google personalises Map Pack results partly on real-time signals. The plumber who shows 'Open now', has recent reviews from this week, and an up-to-date out-of-hours phone number ranks above the one whose GBP says 'closed' at 8pm.

subheadings.title: Tactical implications
list: GBP hours should reflect actual emergency cover — if you take 10pm calls, set hours accordingly
Add 'Open 24 hours' if you genuinely offer 24/7 — Google will surface you for 'open now' filters
Use GBP Posts to advertise out-of-hours availability — these show in Map Pack expanded view
Phone number should be a real mobile, answered, not a routing service that drops calls

sections.heading: The Plumber Keyword Map by Intent
content: Not all plumbing queries are equal. Treating 'plumber [city]' the same as 'emergency plumber [city]' is the most common targeting mistake. Different queries need different pages, different schema and different CTAs.

subheadings.title: Emergency intent (Map Pack dominant, immediate conversion)
content: The searcher has water on the floor. They're picking the first credible Map Pack result.
list: emergency plumber [city]
24 hour plumber near me
burst pipe [city]
no hot water plumber

blocked drain emergency

list: plumber near me
local plumber [city]
plumber today [city]
weekend plumber [city]

subheadings.title: Booked service intent (organic dominant)

list: boiler installation [city]
bathroom installation [city]

central heating installation

subheadings.title: Research / information intent (blog content)

sections.heading: Google Business Profile: The Categories Most Plumbers Get Wrong
content: GBP categories are the single biggest Map Pack ranking lever for plumbers. They tell Google which queries you should appear for. Most plumbers set primary as 'Plumber' and leave it there — missing 60% of the queries they could rank for.
The fix takes 10 minutes and often moves rankings within 2-3 weeks.

subheadings.title: Recommended GBP category setup
list: Primary category: Plumber (this is your default identity)
Secondary: Emergency Plumber Service (unlocks 'emergency plumber' queries)
Secondary: Drainage Service (if you do drains)
Secondary: Boiler Service (if you do gas)
Secondary: Bathroom Remodeler (if you do installs)
Secondary: Heating Contractor (if you do central heating)

subheadings.title: Other GBP wins most plumbers miss
list: Services section: list every service individually (Boiler Repair, Boiler Installation, Tap Repair, etc.) — each one is a ranking signal
Products section: list specific boiler brands you install (Worcester, Vaillant, Ideal)
Photos uploaded weekly — Google rewards active profiles
Q&A: pre-populate the top 5 questions with answers (don't leave it for customers to ask)
Booking link directly to your phone or booking form, not a homepage

sections.heading: The 10-15 Mile Service Area Rule
content: Plumbers love a wide service area. 'I cover the whole of Greater Manchester' sounds like more business. In Map Pack terms, it costs you business.

Google's Map Pack heavily weights proximity. A service area set to 30 miles dilutes your proximity signal across that entire radius. The result: you rank for nothing strongly outside your immediate postcode.

subheadings.title: Service area guidance for UK cities
list: Major cities (Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds, Bristol): 8-12 mile radius maximum
London: 5-8 miles maximum — anything wider gets killed by proximity competition
Smaller towns and rural: 15-20 miles is workable
If you need wider coverage, set up multiple GBPs at different physical addresses (with genuine premises — fake addresses get banned)

sections.heading: Schema Markup: The Quick Technical Win Most Plumbers Skip
content: Almost no UK plumber websites have proper schema markup. Adding LocalBusiness and Service schema correctly is a one-time technical job that produces measurable ranking lift within 4-6 weeks.

subheadings.title: Schema essentials for a plumber site
list: LocalBusiness (or Plumber) schema on the homepage and contact page — NAP, hours, geo coordinates, service area
Service schema on each service page — name of service, area served, provider
FAQPage schema on every page with FAQs (and every service page should have FAQs)
AggregateRating schema linking to your Google reviews
BreadcrumbList schema on internal pages

sections.heading: The Page Architecture That Actually Ranks
content: Most plumber websites have a homepage, an 'About' page, a 'Services' page listing everything in bullets, and a 'Contact' page. That structure cannot rank for the queries that pay.
You need separate pages for each service-intent query, and separate pages for each meaningful location you serve.

subheadings.title: Service pages every plumber should have
list: /emergency-plumber-[city] — dedicated emergency page, phone number above fold, 'we'll be there in [time]' promise, what's included
/boiler-installation-[city] — pricing range, brands fitted, finance options, warranty
/boiler-repair-[city] — same-day promise, common faults, pricing structure
/blocked-drains-[city] — CCTV survey mention, jet washing, pricing
/bathroom-installation-[city] — gallery, process, timeline
/power-flush-[city] — what it is, when you need it, cost
/landlord-gas-safety-certificate-[city] — pricing, turnaround

subheadings.title: Location pages
content: If you cover multiple distinct areas, build a location page for each. Each one needs unique content — not the same template with the place name swapped.
list: Mention local landmarks and neighbourhoods within that area
Reference specific local plumbing characteristics (e.g. older terraces with lead pipes, new-builds with combi systems)
Embed a Google Map of the location
Include 2-3 reviews from clients in that area

sections.heading: Case Study: How a Manchester Plumber Went from #14 to Map Pack Position 1
content: A Manchester-based plumber came to us ranking #14 for 'emergency plumber Manchester'. Three months in business, decent website, no enquiries from Google.
Here's exactly what we changed and what happened.

subheadings.title: What we changed in weeks 1-2
list: GBP categories — added Emergency Plumber Service, Drainage Service, Heating Contractor as secondaries
GBP services — listed 14 individual services instead of 3
Built a dedicated /emergency-plumber-manchester page (1,400 words, FAQ schema, phone number above fold)
Added LocalBusiness and Service schema to the whole site
Service area reduced from 25 miles to 10 miles to recover proximity signal

subheadings.title: What we did in weeks 3-6
list: Built 8 local citations on UK directories (Yell, FreeIndex, Checkatrade, MyBuilder, Bark, Trustatrader, plus 2 Manchester-specific business directories)
Set up a review request workflow — every completed job triggered a text request 2 hours after
Published 3 supporting blog posts (boiler repair vs replacement, signs you need an emergency plumber, what to do when a pipe burst) with internal links to the emergency page

subheadings.title: The results
list: Week 6: hit Map Pack position 3 for 'emergency plumber Manchester'
Week 10: hit Map Pack position 1 for emergency queries, top 3 organic for 5 service terms
Month 3: client attributed 11 new jobs per month to organic search (tracked via 'how did you hear about us')
At an average £220 per job, that's £2,420/month in attributable revenue from organic — against an SEO spend of around £900/month

sections.heading: Reviews: The Plumber's Compounding Asset
content: Plumber reviews compound. Every review is a Map Pack signal, a trust signal for the searcher, and (often) a long-tail keyword if the customer mentions the problem they had ('he fixed our burst pipe at 11pm').
Most plumbers ask for reviews verbally, the customer forgets, and the moment is lost. The fix is automation.

subheadings.title: Review workflow that works
list: Send a text within 2 hours of job completion — never wait until the next day
Use a short link directly to your Google review form (g.page/r/[your-id]/review)
Keep the message personal and short: 'Hi [name], thanks for letting us sort the [problem] today. If we did a good job, a quick Google review really helps — [link]'
Respond to every review within 24 hours, including negatives
Aim for 2-4 new reviews per week minimum — recency matters as much as volume

sections.heading: Internal Linking: How to Tell Google You Own [Service] in [City]
content: Google understands relationships through internal links. If your /boiler-installation page and your /manchester page never link to each other, Google has no signal that you do boiler installation in Manchester.

Every service page should link to every location page with descriptive anchor text. Every location page should link to every service page. Blog posts should link into the relevant service and location pages.

sections.heading: The Mistakes Killing Your Plumber Rankings Right Now
content: Almost every plumber site we audit has at least four of these issues. Fix them and you're already ahead of 80% of competitors.
list: One generic 'Services' page instead of one page per service
GBP set to 'Plumber' only, no secondary categories
Service area set wider than 15 miles
Phone number as an image (not clickable on mobile)
No schema markup at all
Inconsistent NAP across GBP, website and directories
No reviews from the last 90 days
Asking for reviews verbally rather than via automated text
Identical content on multiple location pages (just place name swapped)
No emergency service page despite advertising emergency cover

faqs.question: How much does SEO for plumbers cost in the UK?
faqs.answer: Most UK plumber SEO retainers sit between £600 and £1,500 per month. A single-city plumber targeting emergency and core services typically needs £700-£1,000/month for 6-9 months. Multi-location plumbing companies covering several cities usually invest £1,200-£2,000/month.

faqs.question: How long does plumber SEO take to produce calls?
faqs.answer: Map Pack movement from GBP optimisation and schema can produce a measurable lift in calls within 4-8 weeks. Full top-3 ranking for competitive emergency terms usually takes 3-6 months in major cities. The first leading indicator is GBP impressions and calls — those rise weeks before organic positions do.

faqs.question: How do I rank in the Google Map Pack for plumbing searches?
faqs.answer: Three things matter most: GBP categories set correctly (Plumber primary, Emergency Plumber Service as a secondary), proximity (service area no wider than 10-15 miles in UK cities), and prominence (reviews — aim for 4.7+ stars with recent reviews every week).

faqs.question: Do I need a separate page for emergency plumbing?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it's one of the highest-impact changes you can make. 'Emergency plumber' searches are a different query class with different intent — a generic 'Services' page can't rank for them. A dedicated emergency page with FAQ schema, your phone number above the fold and clear out-of-hours availability outranks generic competitors quickly.

faqs.question: What's the most common SEO mistake plumbers make?
faqs.answer: Setting their service area too wide. Plumbers think a 25-mile radius means more business — Google sees it as a diluted location signal and ranks them for nothing strongly. Cutting the service area to 10-15 miles in most UK cities often improves rankings within weeks.

faqs.question: Is paid Google Ads better than SEO for plumbers?
faqs.answer: They serve different timeframes. Google Ads delivers calls from day one but stops the moment you stop paying — and competitive emergency keywords now cost £8-£25 per click in major UK cities. SEO takes 2-4 months to start producing, but compounds: a Map Pack position 1 ranking continues generating calls without per-click cost. Most successful plumbing businesses run both.
